c: Who am I? — Doris Lessing’s 1962 novel in which a writer keeps four coloured journals, black, red, yellow and blue, plus a fifth to bring her fragmented life together.
“If I am out of my mind, it’s all right with me.” A twice-divorced professor writes unsent letters to the living and the dead in Saul Bellow’s 1964 novel.
Who am I? — Walker Percy’s novel of a New Orleans stockbroker who drifts through Mardi Gras week, seeking a way out of everydayness he calls the search.

A Creole heiress, island born, / A husband cold, a name unsworn;
The madwoman in another’s tale / Is given voice, and burns the vale.
Who am I? — A 1931 experimental novel of six friends whose soliloquies chart a day from sunrise to sunset, with italic interludes of the sea.
“Different sex, same person.” A nobleman born in Elizabeth’s reign wakes up a woman in Constantinople and lives on for centuries in Woolf’s mock-biography.
Who am I? — A Virginia Woolf novel in three parts about a Hebridean summer house, a promised boat trip, a decade of absence and a painter finishing her canvas.

A novelist, a married wife, / A V-1 bomb, a vow for life;
He hates a God he doubts exists, / While Sarah’s love is what persists.
Who am I? — Graham Greene’s thriller about a teenage razor-gang boss, Pinkie, a Catholic seaside murder and a woman named Ida who won’t let it go.
Who am I? — A country gentleman, abandoned by his wife, is trapped in the Amazon forest by a madman who wants the books read aloud forever.
Who am I? — Evelyn Waugh’s farce in which the wrong William Boot is sent to cover an African civil war for the Daily Beast.
Who am I? — Malcolm Lowry’s tale of a British consul’s last day, the Day of the Dead in Cuernavaca, in a haze of mescal.

A boy who stopped his growth at three, / Beats a toy drum rhythmically;
His scream shatters glass in Danzig’s day, / While Nazi flags are on display.
Who am I? — A young engineer visits a cousin at a Swiss tuberculosis sanatorium for three weeks and stays seven years, in Thomas Mann’s novel.
Who am I? — A Lübeck merchant dynasty declines across four generations in Mann’s first novel.
Who am I? — A Hermann Hesse novel of a middle-aged outsider who finds a pamphlet that calls him half-man, half-wolf, and attends a Magic Theatre.
Who am I? — A future province of Castalia where an intellectual order plays a game that synthesises all arts and sciences, until its Magister Ludi leaves.

A surveyor summoned to a snowy town, / Can never reach the lord’s high crown;
The officials write and wait and shirk, / An unfinished tale of Kafka’s work.
Who am I? — Franz Kafka’s unfinished first novel in which a sixteen-year-old exile, Karl Rossmann, arrives in New York and ends up at an Oklahoma theatre.
Who am I? — Robert Musil’s unfinished epic about Ulrich and the Parallel Campaign in dying Austria-Hungary.
Who am I? — Hermann Broch’s trilogy whose three parts, set in 1888, 1903 and 1918, trace the disintegration of European values.
Who am I? — Alfred Döblin’s 1929 montage novel of Franz Biberkopf, a released convict trying to live honestly in Weimar’s capital.

A hero saved an emperor’s life, / His grandson’s lost in garrison strife;
The empire fades in violins, / As Roth records where Trotta’s kin.
Who am I? — Ivo Andrić’s chronicle of a Bosnian town at Višegrad, as seen from a stone span built under Ottoman rule across four centuries.
“If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.” A Sicilian prince watches his class give way in the Risorgimento.
Who am I? — Alessandro Manzoni’s historical novel of two Lombard peasants kept apart by a petty tyrant, set during the Spanish rule and plague of Milan.

w: IF ON A WINTER'S NIGHT A TRAVELER
c: Who am I? — Italo Calvino’s novel addressed to You the Reader, whose ten beginnings are interrupted before each can proceed.

A Venetian tells a Khan of towns, / Zaira, Zenobia, and the crowns;
Each one a thread of memory, / Of Polo’s lone geography.
Who am I? — Umberto Eco’s novel in which three Milanese editors invent a vast conspiracy that begins to take on a life of its own.
Who am I? — Julio Cortázar’s novel offers two ways to read it: straight through, or by hopping according to a table of instructions.
Who am I? — Juan Rulfo’s short novel of a man who travels to the town of Comala to find his father, and discovers it is populated by murmuring ghosts.
Who am I? — Carlos Fuentes’s novel in which a dying Mexican tycoon recalls the key moments of his life, narrated in three voices, I, you and he.

A brothel on a Peruvian plain, / A convent, rubber, jungle’s rain;
Vargas Llosa’s tangled braid, / Of times and lives in Piura’s shade.
Who am I? — A Vargas Llosa novel in which two men drink in a Lima bar and discuss how Peru went wrong under Odría.
Who am I? — Alejo Carpentier’s composer journeys up the Orinoco to find a primitive instrument and time itself.
Who am I? — Alejo Carpentier’s novel of Haiti’s revolution, in which a slave named Ti Noël witnesses Mackandal’s fire and Christophe’s citadel.
Who am I? — Guillermo Cabrera Infante’s pun-laden novel of nightlife in pre-revolutionary Havana, told by many voices.

A Cuban boy with breathing pain, / Wanders through a memory’s rain;
Lezama Lima writes in style baroque, / Of José Cemí’s family’s clock.
Who am I? — Antonio Di Benedetto’s novel of a colonial magistrate in eighteenth-century Paraguay waiting for a transfer that never comes.
Who am I? — Ernesto Sabato’s novel of Martín and Alejandra in Buenos Aires, with a nightmarish chapter on the blind.
Who am I? — A fragmentary autobiography attributed to Bernardo Soares, a Lisbon bookkeeper, written by Fernando Pessoa.
Who am I? — José Saramago’s novel of an unexplained white sickness spreading through a city, and of a doctor’s wife who alone can still see.

A priest builds a flying machine, / Of amber, wills and iron seen;
A one-armed soldier and his love, / Collect the wills of those above.
Who am I? — Eça de Queirós’s epic of a Lisbon family in the 1870s, ending in a tragic revelation about a brother and sister.
Who am I? — Machado de Assis’s narrator spends a book trying to decide if his wife’s eyes were those of a gypsy girl who deceived him.

w: THE POSTHUMOUS MEMOIRS OF BRAS CUBAS
c: Who am I? — Machado de Assis’s novel narrated by a dead man writing from beyond the grave, whose chapters can be a single sentence.

w: THE DEVIL TO PAY IN THE BACKLANDS
c: Who am I? — João Guimarães Rosa’s monologue of Riobaldo, a former jagunço who tells a stranger about his pact and the love he felt for Diadorim.

A sculptor in a maid’s bare room, / Finds a cockroach in the gloom;
Clarice Lispector’s mystic strain, / Records her eating of its brain.
Who am I? — Yasunari Kawabata’s novel of a wealthy Tokyo dilettante who visits a hot-spring town in the mountains to see a geisha.
Who am I? — An ageing Kamakura businessman fears death while watching his son’s marriage fail.
Who am I? — An eleventh-century Japanese work, often called the first novel, about a shining prince of the imperial court and his many loves.

w: THE SAILOR WHO FELL FROM GRACE WITH THE SEA
c: Who am I? — Yukio Mishima’s story of a thirteen-year-old in Yokohama, his gang of boys, and a widow’s lover from a merchant ship.

w: THE TEMPLE OF THE GOLDEN PAVILION
c:
A stammering acolyte in Kyoto, / Obsessed with beauty’s fatal glow;
He sets the shrine of gold ablaze, / Based on a true monk’s wartime days.
Who am I? — Osamu Dazai’s novel of Yozo Oba, who masks himself with clowning and writes three notebooks of shame.
“We are the last of the nobility.” Osamu Dazai’s tale of an aristocratic family in decline in postwar Japan, told through a daughter’s diary.
Who am I? — Haruki Murakami’s novel of a Tokyo man who loses his cat, descends into a dry well and meets the mysterious May Kasahara.
Who am I? — Cao Xueqin’s eighteenth-century Chinese novel of the rise and fall of the Jia clan, with Baoyu, Daiyu and Baochai at its centre.

w: THE PLUM IN THE GOLDEN VASE
c:
A merchant with six wives at hand, / Spreads through Qing’s licentious land;
A racy classic, ill-reputed, / From Water Margin’s tale diluted.
Who am I? — Qian Zhongshu’s satirical novel of a Chinese scholar who returns from Europe with a fake degree, and of marriage as a city under siege.
Who am I? — Gao Xingjian’s novel of a man who travels across rural China after a misdiagnosis of lung cancer, in shifting pronouns.
Who am I? — Chinua Achebe’s novel of Ezeulu, priest of Ulu, in an Igbo village in the 1920s.
Who am I? — Amos Tutuola’s 1952 Yoruba-inflected fantasy of a man who goes to the Land of the Dead in search of his tapster.

w: SEASON OF MIGRATION TO THE NORTH
c: Who am I? — Tayeb Salih’s Sudanese novel in which a narrator returns from studies in England and meets the mysterious Mustafa Sa’eed.

A Zulu priest, a Johannesburg train, / A son who vanished in the rain;
Alan Paton’s plea for South Africa, / For a land of fear and compassion.
Who am I? — J. M. Coetzee’s novel of a Cape Town professor of Romantic poetry, dismissed after an affair, who moves to his daughter’s farm.
Who am I? — A frontier magistrate in an unnamed empire opposes the Colonel’s torture of nomad prisoners.

w: LIFE AND TIMES OF MICHAEL K
c: Who am I? — Coetzee’s novel of a harelipped gardener who pushes his dying mother across a civil-war South Africa in a wheelbarrow.
Who am I? — V. S. Naipaul’s comic masterpiece of a Trinidadian Indian who spends his whole life trying to own his own home.

A trader on a central African shore, / Where boats come to the water’s door;
Naipaul’s Salim sees the Big Man’s rise, / And loses the home before his eyes.
Who am I? — Vikram Seth’s 1993 novel of four families and a mother’s search for a husband for Lata in post-Partition India.
Who am I? — Amitav Ghosh’s novel of a family split between Calcutta and Dhaka, and of a cousin who dies in a riot.
Who am I? — Khushwant Singh’s 1956 novel of the village of Mano Majra, whose peace is shattered when a carriage of corpses arrives in 1947.
Who am I? — Mulk Raj Anand’s 1935 novel of Bakha, a latrine sweeper, whose single day reveals the cruelty of caste.

A tourist leader in Malgudi’s town, / Is jailed, then mistaken for a swami’s crown;
He fasts to bring the rain along, / And ends where saints and sinners throng.
Who am I? — R. K. Narayan’s collection of stories set in an imaginary South Indian town, including Swami and his friends.
Who am I? — Premchand’s last full novel, of the peasant Hori who dreams of owning a cow and dies in debt.
Who am I? — Bankim Chandra Chatterjee’s 1882 novel of an ascetic order in the Bengal famine, which contains the song ‘Vande Mataram’.
Who am I? — Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay’s 1917 novel about a young man who drinks himself to death after losing his childhood love, Paro.

A boy named Apu, a sister Durga, / A railway seen in village fields;
Bibhutibhushan’s song of road, / Of poverty and nature’s load.
Who am I? — Rabindranath Tagore’s novel, told in three voices, of Bimala, her husband Nikhil and his friend Sandip, the firebrand of the Swadeshi movement.
Who am I? — Tagore’s novel of a fervent orthodox Hindu nationalist who learns that he was born Irish, of foreign parents.
Who am I? — Sartre’s 1938 novel of Antoine Roquentin, a historian in Bouville, who stares at a chestnut tree root and discovers the horror of existing.
Who am I? — Camus’s final novel, a confession by a former Paris lawyer, now a judge-penitent in an Amsterdam bar called Mexico City.

A port in Algeria, rats arrive, / A doctor works to keep alive;
The gates are closed, the tally grows, / Camus’s town is full of woes.
Who am I? — Françoise Sagan’s debut, written at eighteen, of a girl on the Riviera who schemes to break up her father’s engagement.
Who am I? — Flann O’Brien’s black comedy of a nameless narrator, a box, and a police station where the law of atoms is bent.
Who am I? — Flann O’Brien’s Dublin novel in which a student writes about an author who writes about characters who rebel against him.
Who am I? — J. P. Donleavy’s picaresque novel of Sebastian Dangerfield, an American law student in Dublin, who drinks and sponges.

A man who ties himself to a chair, / To rock until his mind goes bare;
Samuel Beckett’s first novel, spun / Of London, Cooper, and the sun.
Who am I? — Beckett’s first novel in his French trilogy, in which a crippled man on a bicycle searches for his mother, followed by Moran’s hunt for him.
Who am I? — Beckett’s novel of a servant in Mr Knott’s house whose language is gradually undone by permutations.
Who am I? — The second book in Beckett’s trilogy, in which a bedridden old man tells stories while awaiting his end with a pencil.
Who am I? — Beckett’s last volume in the trilogy, a voice that goes on saying that it can’t go on, in a jar outside a chophouse.

A V-2 rocket’s arc on high, / Slothrop’s hunch of how and why;
Pynchon’s epic, wartime, vast, / Of rockets, Pavlov, paranoia’s cast.
Who am I? — William Gaddis’s 1955 debut novel about a forger named Wyatt Gwyon and the counterfeit nature of modern art.
“War is god.” Cormac McCarthy’s nineteenth-century western of a runaway known as the kid and the scalp-hunting Judge Holden.
Who am I? — Cormac McCarthy’s Knoxville novel of a man who left his family to live on a houseboat among drunks, fishermen and thieves.
Who am I? — John Barth’s mock-epic of Ebenezer Cooke, a poet who sails to Maryland as laureate and is embroiled in a tobacco farce.

A child raised in a university herd, / Is hailed as Grand Tutor by the word;
Barth’s allegory of the Cold War, / Of campus as the planet’s core.
Who am I? — Nabokov’s novel in the form of a 999-line poem by John Shade, with a deranged foreword and commentary by Charles Kinbote.
Who am I? — Nabokov’s saga of Van and Ada Veen, siblings, on the planet Antiterra.
Who am I? — Nabokov’s last Russian novel, of Fyodor, an émigré poet in Berlin who writes a biography of Chernyshevsky.
Who am I? — Nabokov’s 1935 novel of Cincinnatus C., sentenced to death for gnostic turpitude and awaiting an execution whose date nobody will tell him.

A father and daughter wed in turn, / A prince and Charlotte’s ties unlearned;
Henry James’s last great book, / Of flaws that hide beneath a look.
Who am I? — Henry James’s novel of Lambert Strether, who is sent from Woollett, Massachusetts to Paris to retrieve a young man from an entanglement.
Who am I? — Edith Wharton’s New England novel of Charity Royall, who falls for an architect in a village called North Dormer.
Who am I? — Kate Chopin’s 1899 novel of Edna Pontellier, a Creole wife who learns to swim and slowly lets go of the life society expects.

w: MAGGIE: A GIRL OF THE STREETS
c: Who am I? — Stephen Crane’s 1893 novella of a Bowery girl whose illusions fade after a seduction by a bartender.

A dentist in San Francisco’s Polk, / A canary, a wife who won’t joke;
Frank Norris’s hoard of gold, / Ends in Death Valley, hot and cold.
Who am I? — Upton Sinclair’s 1906 novel of a Lithuanian immigrant, Jurgis Rudkus, in Chicago’s Packingtown, which led to food-safety law.
Who am I? — John Dos Passos’s 1925 collage of New York lives, titled for a railway station.
Who am I? — Hemingway’s 1926 novel of expatriates travelling from Paris to the fiesta at Pamplona, with war-wounded Jake and Brett Ashley.
Who am I? — F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel of Dick Diver, a psychiatrist on the Riviera, whose marriage to a wealthy patient slowly disintegrates.

A man who built a hundred plot, / Of Yoknapatawpha’s fatal lot;
Sutpen’s design and Quentin’s ear, / Retell a South that disappears.
Who am I? — Faulkner’s novel of the Bundren family’s journey to bury Addie in Jefferson, told in fifty-nine chapters by fifteen voices.
“Memory believes before knowing remembers.” Faulkner’s tale of Lena Grove, the preacher Hightower and the doomed Joe Christmas.
Who am I? — Richard Wright’s 1940 novel of Bigger Thomas, a young Black man in Chicago, who accidentally kills his employer’s daughter.
Who am I? — Ralph Ellison’s novel of an unnamed narrator who lives in a basement lit by 1,369 bulbs, telling how he came to be unseen.

A pear tree bloom, a muck-black ground, / A hurricane, a rabid hound;
Janie’s three husbands, Tea Cake’s days, / Zora Hurston’s Florida plays.
Who am I? — Bernard Malamud’s novel of Yakov Bok, a Jewish handyman in tsarist Kiev, falsely accused of a ritual murder.
Who am I? — Saul Bellow’s novel of Charlie Citrine, a Pulitzer winner in Chicago, remembering his poet friend.
Who am I? — Saul Bellow’s 1953 picaresque of a Chicago boy who takes any job, from eagle trainer to merchant seaman, and refuses to be fixed.
Who am I? — Margaret Laurence’s novel of ninety-year-old Hagar Shipley, a proud Manitoba matriarch, who flees her son’s house to see her life afresh.

A woman returns to a northern lake, / To find her father, for her sake;
Atwood’s dive beneath the waves, / Brings back what memory saves.
Who am I? — Patrick White’s novel of a German explorer who leads an expedition across the Australian desert in 1845, bound to a young woman in Sydney.
Who am I? — Patrick White’s novel of the painter Hurtle Duffield, who lives for his vision and exploits those around him.
Who am I? — Iris Murdoch’s novel in which the retired tax inspector Bradley Pearson falls in love with a young woman, Julian, daughter of a rival novelist.
Who am I? — John Fowles’s Lyme Regis novel in which a narrator intrudes in 1867 and offers more than one ending.

w: A DANCE TO THE MUSIC OF TIME
c:
Twelve volumes, Powell’s long parade, / Of Nick Jenkins’s social grade;
A painting by Poussin gave the name, / Of seasons, hours and fate’s own game.
